title: The Ladder of Inference
author: Chris Bekins
summary: Bekins introduces the Ladder of Inference, a model for how humans process information and make decisions—and how cognitive biases warp the process. The ladder has seven rungs: start with observable data, select which data to pay attention to, add meaning based on culture and experience, make assumptions, draw conclusions, adopt beliefs, and finally, take actions based on those beliefs. The problem is that we move up the ladder quickly and unconsciously, and we rarely return to question our data selection or meaning-making. Two people observing the same event select different data (confirmation bias), attach different meanings (cultural lens), and reach opposite conclusions—each convinced of their objectivity. Leaders make decisions based on inferences they treat as facts, then defend those decisions without revisiting the rungs below. The Ladder of Inference makes this process visible. By purposefully slowing down and moving through the steps of decision-making, leaders can catch bias and error before they become action. The key moves are: pause at the data rung and ask what you are observing versus assuming; examine the meanings you are adding and ask if culture or past experience is coloring them; state assumptions explicitly and test them; and only then draw conclusions. This practice is uncomfortable because it exposes how much of our 'objectivity' is actually interpretation. But it is also powerful: leaders who practice this thinking become more effective because they notice their own blind spots and invite others to do the same, building a culture of shared inquiry rather than defensive assumption.
points: Decision-making is not objective; we move quickly up the Ladder of Inference, selecting data, adding meaning, and drawing conclusions while treating our inferences as facts.
Two people observing the same event select different data, attach different meanings, and reach opposite conclusions—each convinced of their objectivity.
Leaders move up the ladder unconsciously and rarely return to question which data they selected or what meanings they added, making biased decisions feel like logic.
Slowing down and moving through the rungs deliberately—observing, selecting, adding meaning, assuming, concluding—allows leaders to catch bias and error before they become action.
The practice is uncomfortable but powerful: leaders who examine their inferences become more effective and build cultures of shared inquiry rather than defensive assumption.
